title: Penny and Soot's Ribbon Surprise
markdown:
Once upon a time, in a cozy little stable near a quiet meadow, lived Penny the pony. Her coat was the colour of warm honey, and her mane was as soft as silk. Every day she stepped out into the sunshine. Her hooves made soft thuds on the ground. She loved to gently bump the farmer's hand. Her days were full of grass and a game called follow-the-butterfly in the tall green. She liked her quiet days. The sun felt warm on her back. She loved the sweet smell of clover. And always, always nearby, was her dearest friend, Soot.

Soot was a cat, very black and shiny, with eyes like bright green emeralds that saw everything. He spent most of his days napping in the warmest sunbeams. A happy purr rumbled through the stable floor. He would stretch out long and lazy, a small dark shape of pure ease. When Penny was near, his tail twitched. That meant he was ready for fun. He loved how she made even small things feel like an adventure.

Every day, as the sun started to go down, Penny and Soot went to the hayloft. It was a wonderful place. It smelled of dried sunshine and sweet grass. Penny munched happily on stray bits of hay. Soot curled on a soft pile, a small dark shadow. They watched the world from their high spot. Birds flitted by like tiny dancers. Bees hummed. Penny often wondered what the world looked like from high up, just like Soot did.

One day the sky went grey. A far sound like a giant sigh. Then the wind shook the doors, and rain drummed the roof — not a gentle patter, many little running feet. Penny, who did not love loud weather, shifted. Soot stretched and blinked, a little surprised at so much water. Their sunbeam game was cancelled. This was a proper downpour.

They stayed in. Penny stood by the door and listened. Soot sat on hay, tail neat around his paws, watching drops slide the window. Inside was quieter. The drumming still made the afternoon feel long. Penny sighed, and hay-dust danced by her nose.

Then she saw them: little dusty marks on the loft floor. Like tiny shoe prints. Penny did not wear shoes. Like hoofprints, but smaller and lighter than hers. They led from her usual place toward a darker corner.

She took a slow step. Soot slipped down and followed, quiet as thought. The marks went into stacked hay and low light, a hidden spot. Penny's heart gave a happy jump. Soot's better night-eyes found a plank at the back wall, half lost in straw. His whiskers worked.

Penny pushed the plank with her nose. It creaked, as if waking. Another push, and it opened on an old metal box, rusty and strong. Not gold. Better: a pile of old ribbons, every colour, soft, loosely tied, smelling of flowers and leftover sun. Penny's neigh came out happy and small in the loft.

The stormy afternoon turned into a game. Rain on the roof became their music. Penny nosed the box into the open. Ribbons spilled. Soot batted a long blue one, eyes bright. She untied with careful teeth. He sorted with quick paws. They tied colours to the poles and let them wave. The rest-place looked like a party. Penny's coat took the light. Soot chased a red ribbon that would not quite be caught.

When the rain eased and a little sunshine came through the clouds, making a soft line on the hay, Penny and Soot sat together among their colourful decorations. The tin of ribbons lay open, proof of a rainy-day looking. Penny leaned her head against Soot's soft fur and felt the gentle vibration of his happy purr. The ribbons, a rainbow, were scattered around them, faded fabric soft under hoof and paw, carrying a faint sweet scent of lavender and forgotten sunshine. They had found a treasure, yes. The better part was the sharing, the warm ordinary fun. The world outside was still a little wet. Inside, their loft was bright.

Ever since then, the hayloft held not just hay, but ribbons waiting on afternoons when the sun stayed away.
